changes.old: ## OpenThoughts: вопросы, ответы и выбор учителя
changes.new: ## Phi: selecting code, generating textbooks, and constructing exercises A repository file can be valid Python without providing enough context to learn what its functions do. It may import project-specific classes, set configuration values, or contain one fragment of a larger program. Phi-1 addresses this problem in two separate ways: it selects existing material for educational value and generates additional explanations and exercises. These operations produce different datasets and occur at different stages of training. The following account follows Gunasekar et al., [Textbooks Are All You Need, v2, §2](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.11644v2#S2). The original article and the reproduced figure are licensed CC BY 4.0. ### Phi-1: three datasets, two training stages The authors start with over 35 billion tokens of Python and StackOverflow material. GPT-4 annotates the educational value of approximately 100,000 samples. A random forest then predicts that label using embeddings from a pretrained CodeGen model. GPT-4 therefore supplies labels for a filter; it is not the generator of every training document. The selected corpus contains about 6 billion tokens. GPT-3.5 separately generates less than 1 billion tokens of explanatory Python textbooks, varying the requested topics and target audiences. These two sources form CodeTextbook, the pretraining corpus. A third dataset, CodeExercises, contains less than 180 million tokens of function descriptions and solutions. GPT-3.5 generates these exercises with constraints on function names to vary the tasks. The base model is subsequently fine-tuned on them. | Dataset | Origin | Training role | |---|---|---| | Filtered code-language | Existing Python and StackOverflow samples selected by a classifier | Pretraining | | Synthetic textbooks | Generated prose interleaved with relevant code | Pretraining | | CodeExercises | Generated function descriptions and implementations | Subsequent fine-tuning | The distinction can be inspected in an exercise from §2.2. Its function returns letters that occur in a word but have not already been guessed; repeated letters appear only once, in their first-occurrence order. For `word="banana"` and `guesses=["a"]`, the loop sees `b`, keeps it, skips every `a`, keeps the first `n`, and skips the second `n`. The result is `["b", "n"]`. This representation supplies the task and its implementation together, rather than a function whose purpose depends on files absent from the training window. ```python # Behavior of the CodeExercises example in Phi-1 §2.2. # Type annotations and the long source docstring are omitted here. def valid_guessing_letters(word, guesses): valid_letters = [] for letter in word: if letter not in guesses and letter not in valid_letters: valid_letters.append(letter) return valid_letters assert valid_guessing_letters("banana", ["a"]) == ["b", "n"] assert valid_guessing_letters("banana", []) == ["b", "a", "n"] assert valid_guessing_letters("banana", ["b", "a", "n"]) == [] assert valid_guessing_letters("", []) == [] ``` The training objective remains next-token prediction. Section 2.3 describes concatenating files with an end-of-text token and taking 2048-token windows. The authors select a base checkpoint after roughly eight passes over CodeTextbook, a little over 50 billion tokens seen. Less than 7 billion tokens of source material and more than 50 billion training tokens are therefore compatible counts. The exercises are a later training stage, not the explanation for all of the base model's performance. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/synthetic-recipes-2026-10-29/phi1-data-ablation.png]] *Original Figure 2.1, Suriya Gunasekar et al., [Textbooks Are All You Need](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.11644v2#S2.F1), CC BY 4.0. Complete original PNG, unchanged.* Within each group, orange denotes the ordinary code corpus, light blue CodeTextbook, and dark blue subsequent CodeExercises fine-tuning. Compare the columns within a group before comparing groups: the middle group has more training tokens than the left, and the right has a larger model. The rightmost base and ordinary-corpus runs also use different budgets: about 51 versus 76 billion tokens. The graph supports the reported recipe, but it is not a fully matched experiment isolating synthetic text alone. CodeTextbook changes both filtering and generation; exercise fine-tuning adds another stage. The reported HumanEval pass@1 is 50.6%, rounded to 51 in the figure. This measures completion of short Python functions, not general chatbot quality. Section 5 also retrains after removing exercises close to HumanEval under embedding and AST-based similarity checks. That addresses more than literal string overlap, without proving that every influence of the benchmark has been excluded. Appendix B reports sensitivity to longer and slightly changed prompts. ### Phi-4: starting from a useful seed rather than an empty prompt Phi-4 uses selected organic material both directly and as seeds for generation. A seed can be an excerpt from a paper, a code fragment, or an existing question. The generation procedure then controls how that material is presented: as an explanation, exercise, conversation, or sequence of reasoning steps. The authors report about 50 broad synthetic dataset types, with different seeds and multi-stage prompting procedures. [Source: Abdin et al., Phi-4, §2](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.08905v1#S2). Their motivation for rewriting includes the order in which information is presented. A human can solve a problem and then edit the final answer into the first sentence. A model trained left to right must predict that answer before seeing the later working. A generated step-by-step solution can put the intermediate information before the result. This is a motivation for the recipe, not a guarantee that generated reasoning is correct or that answer-first text is always unsuitable. The seed-selection and generation stages are also separate: 1. Pages are selected for educational content, then passages are scored for factual and reasoning content. A selected page need not make every one of its passages a useful seed. 2. For question seeds, several independent answers are generated. Questions with complete agreement or completely inconsistent answers are removed to target an intermediate difficulty range. The plurality answer is used for some rejection-sampling procedures. 3. Selected passages are rewritten or expanded. Self-revision prompts ask for criticism and an improved response. Where applicable, code is checked through execution and tests. Agreement in step 2 is a consistency signal, not ground truth. Four copies of the same wrong answer still agree. Conversely, multiple valid methods or ambiguous answer formatting can make a solvable question appear inconsistent. The paper does not provide a universal vote threshold that can be applied to every subject. Instruction reversal changes which part of an example exists first. Given a code fragment, a model writes an instruction that describes it; the stored example puts that instruction before the code. The authors retain examples with high fidelity between original and regenerated code. For instance, an instruction generated for the function above must specify both excluding previous guesses and removing repeated letters. "Return the letters not guessed yet" alone leaves duplicate handling unspecified. Running the four cases checks those cases, not every property of the generated instruction or program. ### Reading the repetition experiment and the final mixture ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/synthetic-recipes-2026-10-29/phi4-repetitions.png]] *Original Figure 2, Marah Abdin et al., [Phi-4 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.08905v1#S3.F2), CC BY 4.0. Complete original PNG, unchanged.* Dashed lines denote 14B models; solid lines denote 7B models. Each size has a four-epoch and a twelve-epoch synthetic-data run. The available synthetic subset is fixed, and the compared runs use the same total token horizon. More repetitions of that subset therefore replace fresh web tokens. The twelve-epoch curves attain higher 5-shot MMLU in these experiments. This does not establish twelve epochs as an optimum, nor measure what would happen if the replacement web corpus were different. The horizontal axis is the authors' checkpoint index, not the number of synthetic epochs. The final pretraining mixture is another result, not a transcription of these four curves. Table 5 separates the fraction of training tokens from the number of available unique tokens: | Source | Training fraction | Unique tokens | Reported epochs | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Web | 15% | 1.3T | 1.2 | | Web rewrites | 15% | 290B | 5.2 | | Synthetic | 40% | 290B | 13.8 | | Code | 20% | 820B | 2.4 | | Acquired sources | 10% | 580B | 1.7 | For an approximately 10T-token horizon, the synthetic row accounts for 4T sampled tokens. Dividing by its 290B-token pool gives about 13.8 epochs. The two rows with 290B available tokens do not get the same exposure: their mixture weights differ. Web rewrites are themselves generated data but are a separate category in this table. The code category contains both synthetic and raw code, so these rows do not identify an exact human-versus-generated fraction for every training token. The earlier figure of about 400B unweighted synthetic tokens in §2.2 describes the generation collection. Table 5 describes the final training categories. The report does not provide a document-level reconciliation of those counts; adding them would double-count rather than establish a larger training corpus. The authors' synthetic-only 13B ablations improve several reasoning benchmarks but lose substantially on TriviaQA. Rewriting web data narrows that loss without removing it. They retain knowledge-heavy web and acquired sources in the final mixture, and note that some pretraining differences shrink after post-training. A single aggregate reasoning score would therefore select a different mixture from a criterion that also values factual knowledge. Detailed family changes and Pivotal Token Search are linked from [[02 Areas/ML & DL/02 Атлас моделей/Семейства/Phi|the Phi entry]]. ## Nemotron-4: generating prompts, dialogues, and preference pairs A synthetic alignment corpus needs more than answers. It needs prompts that cover the intended tasks, demonstrations of conversations, and pairs whose preference labels mean something. NVIDIA's [Nemotron-4 report, §3.1–3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.11704v1#S3) describes these as separate data-generation procedures. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/synthetic-recipes-2026-10-29/nemotron4-prompts.png]] *Original Figure 2, NVIDIA, [Nemotron-4 340B Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.11704v1#S3.F2), CC BY 4.0. The four complete pipelines generate open Q&A, writing, document-grounded Q&A, and math/code prompts, respectively. Original PNG copied without alteration.* For open questions, topics lead to questions and then to more specific revisions. Writing tasks additionally choose a document type. Closed Q&A starts from a C4 document and combines it with a generated instruction. Math and code start from relevant keywords. These choices vary the distribution of tasks before response generation. In the initial iteration, the prompt generator is Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, not necessarily a Nemotron model. Real LMSYS prompts are also included; the corpus is not composed entirely of model-invented user requests. The SFT and preference prompt sets are disjoint. In the SFT split, potentially unsafe LMSYS prompts are removed to avoid eliciting unwanted demonstrations. They remain in the preference split so the model can learn which response to prefer. Removing a prompt from SFT and removing it from every stage of alignment would thus be different policies. For SFT, the generator alternates assistant and user roles to build three-turn conversations. Each generated user turn is conditioned on the history and a requested user personality; post-processing removes formulaic politeness. Dialogue quality is scored and low-scoring examples are filtered. A realistic-looking exchange can still contain wrong facts, so this procedure does not supply the same evidence as executing a test. For preference data, multiple responses come from intermediate models or repeated samples of the strongest available model. When an objective answer or a programmatic verifier exists, correct and incorrect responses can form the chosen/rejected pair. For other tasks, the authors first use an LLM judge twice with the response order swapped, keeping a pair only when the decisions are consistent. They later use the regression reward model to rank responses. For example, let candidates A and B be presented first as `[A, B]` and then as `[B, A]`. If the judge chooses the first position both times, it has selected A and then B; that pair is rejected. If it chooses the first position and then the second, both decisions select A. The consistency check accepts the pair, but cannot establish that A is factually correct. Nemotron-4-340B-Reward predicts five attributes: helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity. Its labels come from the 10K human-annotated HelpSteer2 dataset. A weighted sum can convert those predictions into a ranking score. The attribute named correctness remains a learned estimate; it is not a proof or an executable verifier. The regression model and the pairwise loss used to train a policy are different components, as developed in [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/12 Post-training и Alignment/03 Reward modeling|reward modeling]] and [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/12 Post-training и Alignment/05 DPO|DPO]]. Across iterations, an aligned generator produces data for a stronger base checkpoint, and the resulting aligned model can become the next generator. The report's weak-to-strong procedure also changes base checkpoints while pretraining continues. Its improvement is therefore not an isolated experiment in repeatedly training one fixed model on its own outputs. The reported "over 98%" synthetic share refers to the alignment data, not to the 9T-token base pretraining corpus. Section 3 accounts separately for approximately 20K human-annotated records: 10K for SFT and 10K HelpSteer2 records for reward-model training and preference fine-tuning. Those are annotated examples, not 20,000 seed prompts from which every synthetic record is derived. The distinct Nemotron model lines are indexed in [[02 Areas/ML & DL/02 Атлас моделей/Семейства/Nemotron|the Nemotron entry]]. ## OpenThoughts: вопросы, ответы и выбор учителя

The reported 5.6-point MMLU improvement applies to the high-quality
subset, not to every version of Nemotron-CC. Table 5 compares 8B models
trained for 1T tokens: 73% comes from the tested Common Crawl dataset and
27% from the same fixed non-Crawl mixture.

| Crawl portion | MMLU accuracy | Average across the ten tasks |
|---|---:|---:|
| DCLM | 53.4 | 57.0 |
| Full Nemotron-CC | 53.0 | 57.8 |
| Nemotron-CC-HQ | 59.0 | 60.1 |

Thus 59.0 minus 53.4 gives 5.6 percentage points for the HQ comparison.
The full corpus has a different trade-off: much more unique real data
with roughly similar short-horizon accuracy. Neither comparison isolates
rewriting alone; the data recipe also changes selection and filtering.
The separate 15T-token comparison with Llama 3.1 is another experiment,
not an extension of these 1T runs.
[Source: Su et al., §3.1–3.2 and Table 5](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.123.pdf#page=6).
